chunks: And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Ali from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from Al-Halabi who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'What is the ruling on vegetables (al-khudrah)?' He said, 'And what is it?' I said, 'Sugarcane and watermelon, and similar among the vegetables.' He said, 'There is nothing due on them unless their like is sold for money, and a year passes over it, then zakat is due on it.'

And regarding the fruit trees (shajar al-ghadah) of peaches and apricots and their like, is there zakat on them? He said, 'No.' I said, 'Their value (price)?' He said, 'When a year passes over their price, then purify it (pay zakat).'

key_terms.الْغَضَاة: Fruit trees (specifically those bearing fruit continuously or in seasons)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling of zakat on vegetables and fruits in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the distinction between zakat on agricultural produce (khuruj) and zakat on commercial assets (mal), establishing that vegetables are subject to zakat upon sale and the passage of a lunar year (hawl) over the proceeds. It further specifies that for fruit trees like peaches and apricots, the obligation arises on their market value rather than the fruit itself, reflecting the Shia juristic view on the nature of wealth accumulation in trade. This ruling underscores the principle that zakat on goods is tied to their status as capital assets held for a full year, aligning with the broader Shia methodology of distinguishing between harvest-based and trade-based zakat.
